title: Trump Organization Fined $1.6M After Tax Fraud Conviction
description_medium: On January 13, 2023, a New York judge ordered two Trump Organization affiliates to pay a $1.6 million criminal penalty, the maximum allowed in the case. A jury had found the companies guilty of 17 tax-related charges, including conspiracy and falsifying business records. The case concerned executives’ personal taxes on company perks; Donald Trump himself was not on trial.
description_long: On January 13, 2023, Manhattan judge Juan Merchan sentenced two Trump Organization affiliates to pay a $1.6 million criminal penalty after a jury found them guilty of 17 criminal charges. Reuters reported that the convictions followed a scheme to defraud tax authorities over 15 years, and that the fine was the maximum the judge could impose. The Associated Press described the case as involving senior executives who avoided personal income taxes on benefits such as rent-free apartments, luxury cars, and private-school tuition. The penalty applied to the companies, not Donald Trump personally; he was not on trial in this case. The sentence marked the end of the criminal case against the corporate entities, while the executives’ own conduct and penalties were separate matters. The amount was constrained by the maximum available under law, a limitation prosecutors criticized. The conviction established criminal liability for the affiliates, but it should not be described as a personal conviction of Trump.

title: Trump Organization Ousted from Panama Hotel Branded Trump
description_medium: In March 2018, Trump Organization executives left the management offices of the Trump-branded hotel in Panama City after a 12-day standoff with the property’s owners. The dispute followed the owners’ effort to terminate the company’s management role, which the Trump Organization had contested. Police and a Panamanian judicial official helped the owners take control of the offices; related legal disputes were expected to continue.
description_long: The Trump Organization’s role at a Trump-branded hotel in Panama City ended in a highly visible management dispute in March 2018. The Associated Press, reporting through The Guardian, said executives and security guards left the management offices after a 12-day standoff with the property’s owners. Orestes Fintiklis, the head of the owners’ association, sought to take control on their behalf. The owners had attempted to fire the Trump company the previous year, but it disputed the termination as legally invalid and refused to hand over the property. A Panamanian judicial official and police accompanied Fintiklis into the offices, ending the immediate confrontation. The hotel’s commercial and legal dispute was not necessarily over: the report said litigation and arbitration complaints already existed and that the legal dispute was expected to continue. The episode concerned the company’s management contract and physical control of the property; it was not itself a ruling that resolved every contract claim.

title: Cambridge Analytica Tied to Trump Campaign Data Operations
description_medium: A March 2018 Guardian investigation reported that Cambridge Analytica, which worked with Donald Trump’s 2016 campaign, used Facebook profile data to build voter profiles and target personalized political ads. The reporting relied on whistleblower Christopher Wylie and documents. It described data obtained without users’ authorization, while noting Facebook had learned of large-scale collection earlier.
description_long: A March 2018 investigation by The Guardian reported that Cambridge Analytica harvested Facebook profile information from millions of U.S. voters and used it to build voter profiles for personalized political advertising. The article said the data firm had worked with Donald Trump’s 2016 election team, connecting the company’s data practices to a presidential campaign. Its account drew on whistleblower Christopher Wylie and documents, and described personal information obtained without authorization through a research operation. The report also said Facebook had learned by late 2015 that data had been collected on a large scale but had not notified users and took only limited steps to recover it. These findings raised questions about consent, platform oversight, and political targeting. They do not by themselves establish that the profiles changed individual votes or determined the election result. The originally supplied Britannica page concerns Cambridge, England, not Cambridge Analytica, so it does not support this event; the replacement source is contemporaneous reporting about the firm and data collection.

title: Threatens Tariffs on Allies Over Greenland Bid
description_medium: On January 17, 2026, Donald Trump announced a 10% tariff beginning February 1 on goods from eight European countries, including Denmark, Norway, and Germany, unless a deal allowed the United States to purchase Greenland. He said the rate would rise to 25% on June 1. The announcement was a threat tied to his territorial demand; the report records the proposed schedule, not tariffs already collected.
description_long: On January 17, 2026, President Donald Trump announced that the United States would impose a 10% tariff on goods from Denmark, Norway, Sweden, France, Germany, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, and Finland beginning February 1. He said the rate would rise to 25% on June 1 and remain until a deal was reached for the United States to purchase Greenland. The Guardian reported that Trump linked the threat to the presence of European forces in Greenland and his stated interest in acquiring the autonomous Danish territory. European leaders publicly rejected the pressure and expressed solidarity with Denmark and Greenland; several warned tariffs could damage transatlantic relations. The episode used threatened trade penalties to press an allied group over a territorial demand. At the time of the announcement, these were proposed future tariffs, not proof that duties had already taken effect or been collected. The supplied Guardian link focused on a separate message to Norway’s prime minister; this account relies on the paper’s contemporaneous report specifically covering the tariff announcement.

title: Facebook and Instagram Suspend Trump Indefinitely
description_medium: On January 7, 2021, Facebook announced that it was extending its block on Donald Trump’s Facebook and Instagram accounts indefinitely, and for at least two weeks, after the Capitol attack. Meta said it judged his posts about the attack and election results to contribute to the risk of further violence. The decision was a platform enforcement action, not a government order.
description_long: Facebook and Instagram restricted Donald Trump’s ability to post after the January 6, 2021 attack on the U.S. Capitol. In its January 7 update, Facebook said it was extending the block indefinitely and for at least two weeks because it believed the risks of allowing Trump to continue using the services were too great. The company had removed his recent video about the protests and a subsequent post about election results, explaining that it judged them to contribute to the risk of ongoing violence. Meta’s announcement was a decision under the company’s platform policies, not a court order or government ban. “Indefinite” described the initial suspension rather than its eventual duration: Facebook later referred the decision to its independent Oversight Board, and subsequently imposed a two-year suspension from the original date. That later review is useful context, while the entry’s event remains the initial post-attack restriction. The action curtailed Trump’s access to two major social platforms during the final days of his presidency.
